text: When he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

versions.text: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
versions.explanation: The Greek has only "he opened"; "the Lamb" is an interpretive addition. It is contextually correct (from ch. 6), but if retained it would be better marked in a footnote. Consider either the literal "he" or adding a footnote noting the subject is the Lamb.

text: And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.
Another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne.
And the smoke of the incense rose with the prayers of the saints from the angel's hand before God.
Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth; and there came peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
Then the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to sound them.

The first sounded his trumpet, and there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was hurled down on the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.
The second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain ablaze with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood,
a third of the creatures in the sea, those that had life, died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

versions.text: a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
versions.explanation: The Greek distinguishes "creatures in the sea" from the qualifying phrase "those having life/souls." The current rendering collapses this, though it is acceptable; a slight expansion preserves the fuller sense.

versions.text: a third of the creatures in the sea, the ones having life, died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
versions.explanation: The appositional phrase τὰ ἔχοντα ψυχάς is accurately represented, but "the ones having life" is a wooden participial construction that stumbles when read aloud, especially wedged between subject and verb. "Those that had life" keeps the same distinction while reading more smoothly.

text: The third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star, blazing like a torch, fell from the sky. It fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.
The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned bitter as wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.

The fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them turned dark, and a third of the day had no light, and a third of the night as well.

versions.text: The fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them turned dark. A third of the day was without light, and the night as well.
versions.explanation: The purpose clause (ἵνα) governs both the darkening and the loss of light, so breaking it into a separate sentence weakens the link. Also "and the night as well" should carry the sense "a third of the night likewise."

text: Then I looked, and I heard an eagle flying high overhead call out with a loud voice: "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the blasts of the trumpets about to be sounded by the other three angels!"
